content: 1. The depth of the tremors reported on December 18 ranges from 17 to 23 kilometers. The locations of these tremors are marked with red circles. The white puffs visible over the island are clouds and not volcanic emissions. 2. El Hierro is a shield volcano that is actively growing along the southwestern edge of the ancient El Golfo volcano. The El Golfo volcano collapsed approximately 130,000 years ago. The rugged, reddish-brown terrain of the island is evidence of prolonged volcanic activity in the region. Historical records suggest that El Hierro last erupted in 1793. This area has the highest concentration of young volcanic vents in the Canary Islands. 3. Greenstone belts are geological zones composed of variably metamorphosed mafic to ultramafic volcanic sequences, often associated with sedimentary rocks. These belts are typically found within Archaean and Proterozoic cratons, situated between granite and gneiss formations. The term greenstone originates from the green coloration imparted by metamorphic minerals such as chlorite, actinolite, and other green amphiboles within the mafic rocks. 4. Greenstone belts can range in length from several dozen to several thousand kilometers. Despite their diverse composition of individual rock units, they are considered a distinct stratigraphic grouping, particularly on a continental scale. These belts are distributed throughout geological history, from the Phanerozoic Franciscan belts in California, which include blueschist, whiteschist, and greenschist facies, to the Palaeozoic greenstone belts of the Lachlan Fold Belt in Eastern Australia, as well as numerous Proterozoic and Archaean examples. 5. Archaean greenstones are found in regions such as the Slave Craton in northern Canada, the Pilbara and Yilgarn Cratons in Western Australia, the Gawler Craton in South Australia, and the Wyoming Craton in the United States. Additional examples are located in South and Eastern Africa, including the Kaapvaal Craton, the cratonic core of Madagascar, West Africa, Brazil, northern Scandinavia, and the Kola Peninsula (part of the Baltic Shield). 6. Phanerozoic ophiolite belts and greenstone belts are present in the Franciscan Complex of southwestern North America, the Lachlan Fold Belt, the Gympie Terrane of Eastern Australia, the ophiolite belts of Oman, and around the Guiana Shield. 7. Meteor light curve emissions are generally confined to the height interval of 100 to 110 kilometers and are rarely observed in meteors traveling at velocities below approximately 40 kilometers per second. 8. Moldavite is an olive-green or dull greenish vitreous material, likely formed by a meteorite impact. It is classified as a type of tektite. Due to its difficult fusibility, extremely low water content, and unique chemical composition, the prevailing scientific consensus is that moldavites were formed approximately 15 million years ago during the impact of a giant meteorite in the present-day Nördlinger Ries region. 9. During the impact, molten material was ejected and cooled while airborne, with most of it falling in central Bohemia, an area traversed by the Vltava River. Moldavites have since been discovered in regions including southern Bohemia, western Moravia, the Cheb Basin (northwest Bohemia), Lusatia (Germany), and Waldviertel (Austria). 10. Isotope analysis of moldavite samples has revealed a beryllium-10 isotope composition similar to that of Australasian tektites (australites) and Ivory Coast tektites (ivorites). This similarity suggests that moldavites, australites, and ivorites are composed of near-surface and loosely consolidated terrestrial sediments that were melted by hypervelocity impacts.
